paras: This quote is valid for thirty days. All figures are per year unless the line says otherwise, and nothing is paid upfront: the first payment falls due at the first milestone, not at signature.

The licence fee is twenty-eight thousand a year and covers up to fifty users. Above fifty, the unit price falls by roughly a fifth, so a team of eighty costs less per person than a team of forty. The setup is a one-off fifty-six thousand, which is twice as much as one year of licence and is the largest single figure on this page.

Two options. Option A is one year at a time: eighty-four thousand in year one, and twenty-eight thousand every year after that. It is the cheapest option to leave and the most expensive one to stay in, and it is the right choice if the decision has to be reversible. Option B is a three-year term at nineteen thousand a year with the setup waived. In year one it is a little over half of Option A, and across the three years it is about a third less per year.

On discounts, we would rather be direct. The price above already assumes a partnership rather than a single project, and we do not hold a percentage back to give away later. If the commercial shape has to change, we would prefer to change the term or the scope rather than the number, because a discount given quickly tells you the first price was not real.

items.situation: Compare your annual fee with the competitor's, in one sentence.
tips: Our licence fee is lower than theirs, but the setup costs more.
Short adjective: -er plus than. Never more cheaper.

items.situation: Say that Option A is the least expensive of three, using a short adjective.
tips: Option A is the cheapest of the three.
The plus -est, and of the three, not between the three.

items.situation: Say that the setup is two times one year of licence.
tips: The setup costs twice as much as one year of licence.

items.situation: State the ceiling and the floor of what the price covers.
tips: It covers up to fifty users and at least two integrations.
Up to = maximum. At least = minimum.

items.situation: The customer says the total is too high. What is your first sentence?
tips: Let me break it down: licence, setup and training. Which of the three are we talking about?

items.situation: Offer to remove the setup without giving it away.
tips: We can waive the setup, but only on a three-year term.
The discount buys something: it is not a gift.

listenings.text: I never say the number first. A price with nothing beside it is just a big number, and if you do not give the customer a comparison, they will find their own, and it will be the cheapest thing they can remember. So the sentence before the price is always the comparison: what they spend today, what the problem costs them every month, or what the other option costs over three years. The second habit is breaking it down. Almost everything that looks expensive turns out to be three things, and only one of them is actually being argued about, and once it is on the table in parts, the conversation gets much smaller. And here is a small thing that costs people deals. If you hesitate while you are saying a number, the customer does not hear somebody thinking in a second language. They hear doubt about the price, and then you are negotiating a figure that you yourself have already admitted is too high.

When three quotes land on my desk, people assume I compare them with each other. I do not, or at least not first. My real benchmark is what we pay today, and that number includes the people, which most vendors forget. If your proposal is more expensive than the tool we have and cheaper than the tool plus the two people, then we have something to talk about. If a quote arrives as one number with nothing underneath it, I send it back and ask for a breakdown, and I will tell you honestly what I have learned from doing that for years: the ones who cannot break it down usually cannot defend it either. And the fastest way to lose me is the discount that arrives too early. If fifteen per cent appears before I have even pushed, then the first price was not real, and now I have to check every other number in the document twice.
